scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] Meet the Glessner House.

[short pause] A summer morning, 1904, at 1800 Prairie Avenue. Morning illumination from the lake falls across the granite façade. [short pause] Behind it reside John J. Glessner, an agricultural-machinery executive from Ohio; his wife Frances, a dedicated diarist since 1879; and the residence that scandalized the avenue.

[short pause] Ten stops on foot, completely encircling a single building: the corner, the Eighteenth Street elevation, the alley, the principal entrance, the carriage passage and the interior courtyard. [short pause] The narrative derives predominantly from the owner's own account, composed for his children in 1923. [short pause] Exteriors exclusively.

[short pause] Commence at the corner, where the neighbors first confronted the residence and disapproved of what they observed.
scripts.stop:corner: [wistfully] An antiquated Chicago saying characterized Prairie Avenue as "the sunny street that holds the sifted few". [short pause] Pullman's mansion occupies the diagonal corner, and Kimball's French chateau faces it across the avenue. Then there is this composition: rusticated granite, diminutive recessed windows, precipitous red roofs. [short pause] It was Henry Hobson Richardson's final residential design, and he never witnessed its completion.
scripts.stop:north-wall: [curious] This is the elevation contemporaries criticized when the residence was new. [short pause] Pedestrians remarked upon the narrow windows, "just enough to light the narrow corridors". Richardson maintained that the windows of an urban residence were "not to look out of", since occupants invariably smother them in shades and draperies. [short pause] The architecture deliberately turns its back upon the street.
scripts.stop:arch: [measured] The great arch constitutes the service entrance, where a narrow corridor leads toward the kitchen. [short pause] It also accommodates musical conspiracies. [short pause] On New Year's Day 1903 a double quartet of horns infiltrated through the Eighteenth Street door and ascended the service stairs, and at four o'clock commenced performing in the upper hall.
scripts.stop:stable: [measured] The western wing contains the stable and carriage house, with an expansive carriage doorway onto Eighteenth Street and interior walls of white glazed brick. [short pause] The furnace room occupies the level beneath it, ensuring that the dust, dirt and disturbance associated with coal and ashes never penetrate the residence itself.
scripts.stop:gate: [measured] Around the corner, these alley gates open into the courtyard, and they facilitated an ingenious maneuver. [short pause] On 1 December 1887 the family transported everything through here, "before our neighbors suspected even that we were about to move". [short pause] That evening they kindled the new hearth with live fire carried ceremonially from the previous one.
scripts.stop:door: [measured] The principal entrance: massive oak reinforced with iron straps, with a square window behind an iron grille. [short pause] Richardson prohibited painting the ironwork; it was instead Bower-Barffed against corrosion, a process Glessner never encountered elsewhere. [short pause] The wall appears monolithic, but it is brick veneered with granite slabs, with deep stones at every opening to perpetuate the illusion.
scripts.stop:porte: [playfully] Not every visitor utilizes the principal entrance. [short pause] Here a carriage could depart Prairie Avenue and proceed directly beneath the residence, through two paneled oak doors suspended on massive iron straps, and emerge into a private courtyard. [short pause] Follow its route through.
scripts.stop:court-north: [warmly] Inside, the residence reverses its architectural character. [short pause] From the street it appeared impenetrable; here it opens generously. Richardson positioned expansive windows along this sunny courtyard elevation, admitting, Glessner wrote, "a flood of sunlight when the sun shines in Chicago". [short pause] The principal family rooms orient inward toward this tranquil enclosure rather than outward toward the avenue.
scripts.stop:hall-bow: [measured] The rounded bay above the terrace steps encloses the entrance hall. [short pause] Its courtyard door is glazed with yellow glass beneath chipped white glass, so the interior seems sunlit even on overcast days. [short pause] These vines were transplanted from the family's previous residence; one specimen, fifty-five feet long, was replanted intact, and it flourished.
scripts.stop:family: [warmly] Behind these walls, 1904 is an eventful year. [short pause] Frances Glessner, a diarist since 1879, has installed a silversmith's workbench in the basement, and throughout winter and spring her Monday Morning Reading Class convenes in the library. [short pause] Years earlier her son George and his companions operated a telegraph company from his schoolroom, connected to seven neighboring houses.
scripts.ending:finish: [softly] Richardson never witnessed any of this. [short pause] Approximately three weeks before his death in April 1886, too debilitated to leave his bedroom, he indicated on the drawings where the light fixtures would be installed and informed Glessner, "There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished". [short pause] Excavation commenced that June, and George and Frances turned the ceremonial first soil. [short pause] Glessner remained convinced it was the residence Richardson would most have preferred to inhabit himself.
